Pure beryl is colorless goshenite, and trace elements make the famous varieties: chromium or vanadium for emerald, iron for blue aquamarine and yellow heliodor, manganese for pink morganite. Emerald is usually included and often oiled, while aquamarine can be remarkably clean and large. Collectors prize fine crystals from Colombia, Brazil, Zambia and Pakistan. In crystal tradition beryl is linked with clarity and calm. Explore the group below.

Corundum.description: Corundum family gems: ruby and sapphire in every color. Aluminum oxide at hardness 9, second only to diamond and prized for durability and color.
Corundum.intro: Corundum is aluminum oxide with a hardness of 9, the hardest common mineral after diamond. In its red form chromium makes it ruby, and every other color is called sapphire, including blue, pink, yellow, orange and the rare padparadscha. Star sapphires and star rubies show a six-rayed star caused by tiny needle-like inclusions. Many stones are heat treated to improve color, and the best untreated ones are very valuable. Important sources include Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Madagascar and Montana. Collectors value corundum for its toughness and brilliance. Explore the group below.

Garnet.description: Garnet family gems: almandine, pyrope, spessartine, grossular and more. A varied silicate group best known for deep red but found in many colors.
Garnet.intro: Garnet is not one mineral but a group of related silicates that share a cubic crystal form, often as round, many-faced crystals, with a hardness of about 6.5 to 7.5. The main members are almandine, pyrope, spessartine, grossular, andradite and uvarovite, and they cover almost every color but blue. Deep red is the most familiar, yet orange spessartine, green tsavorite and demantoid are admired by gem buyers. The name is thought to come from a word for pomegranate, because the small red crystals look like seeds. Garnet has been worn since ancient times. Explore the group below.

Tourmaline.description: Tourmaline family gemstones: black schorl, pink rubellite, green verdelite and watermelon crystals. A boron silicate in nearly every color. See the full list.
Tourmaline.intro: Tourmaline is a complex boron silicate that forms long, striated, rounded-triangular crystals with a hardness of 7 to 7.5. It is found in more colors than almost any other gem, from common black schorl to pink rubellite, green verdelite, blue indicolite and bi-colored watermelon crystals. Tourmaline becomes electrically charged when heated or pressed, a property that fascinated early scientists. Collectors prize gem crystals from Brazil, Afghanistan, Nigeria and Maine. In crystal tradition black tourmaline is one of the most popular protective stones. Explore the group below. Prices range from very modest for black schorl to very high for fine Paraiba blue-green stones.

Topaz.description: Topaz family gemstones: imperial, blue, white and mystic topaz. An aluminum fluorosilicate with a hardness of 8 and perfect cleavage. See the full list.
Topaz.intro: Topaz is an aluminum fluorosilicate that crystallizes in the orthorhombic system with a hardness of 8. It has perfect cleavage in one direction, so a hard knock can split a stone. Natural topaz comes in honey, pink, and the prized orange-pink imperial shade, while the pale blue topaz sold today is almost always colorless topaz that has been irradiated and heated. Mystic topaz is coated to give a rainbow sheen. Large, clean crystals come from Brazil, Pakistan, Russia and Sri Lanka. Collectors enjoy the size and clarity of topaz crystals. Explore the group below. Always ask a seller whether a blue stone is treated, since nearly all of it is.

Jade.description: Jade crystals and carvings: jadeite and nephrite, the two stones traditionally called jade, treasured in Asia and Mesoamerica for thousands of years.
Jade.intro: The name jade covers two different minerals: nephrite, a calcium magnesium amphibole, and jadeite, a sodium aluminum pyroxene. Both are tough, fibrous or granular rocks with a waxy, smooth feel, with hardness of about 6 to 7. Nephrite is found in China, New Zealand, Canada and Siberia, while the finest jadeite comes from Myanmar and Guatemala. Jade has been carved into tools, ornaments and ritual objects in China and Mesoamerica for thousands of years, and imperial green jadeite is among the most expensive gem materials. Treated and dyed jade is common, so buying carefully matters. Browse the group below.

Opal.description: Opal family gemstones: precious, fire, common and boulder opal. Hydrated silica with flashing play of color, prized by collectors for centuries.
Opal.intro: Opal is hydrated silica, a noncrystalline mineraloid with a hardness of 5.5 to 6.5 and a water content of up to 10 percent. Precious opal shows play of color, caused by tiny silica spheres that diffract light. Common opal lacks that effect but comes in pastel and earthy shades such as Peruvian blue and pink. Fire opal is warm orange without play of color. Australia produces most of the world's precious opal, with Ethiopia and Mexico also important. Because opal can dry out and crack, collectors take care in storage. Explore the group below.

Spinel.description: Spinel family gemstones: red, pink, blue and black spinel. A magnesium aluminum oxide once mistaken for ruby, now prized in its own right. See the full list.
Spinel.intro: Spinel is a magnesium aluminum oxide that forms neat octahedral crystals in the cubic system, with a hardness of 8. For centuries red spinel was mistaken for ruby, and several famous crown jewels turned out to be spinel. It occurs in red, pink, orange, blue, violet and black, and fine stones are rarer than many buyers realize. Sources include Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Tajikistan and Vietnam. Collectors prize it for its bright color and natural, untreated state. Explore the group below. Its range of colors, clarity and good hardness make it a favorite for jewelry and a rewarding stone to collect.

Chrysoberyl.description: Chrysoberyl family gemstones: alexandrite and cat's eye. A beryllium aluminum oxide at hardness 8.5 known for color change and chatoyancy. See the full list.
Chrysoberyl.intro: Chrysoberyl is a beryllium aluminum oxide with a hardness of 8.5, making it one of the toughest gems. Its two star varieties are alexandrite, which shifts from green in daylight to red in incandescent light, and cat's eye, which shows a bright line of light across a polished cabochon. Alexandrite was first found in Russia's Ural Mountains and named for a young prince, while Brazil, Sri Lanka and India produce much of today's supply. Fine alexandrite is among the most valuable gems in the world. Explore the group below. Collectors also seek rare cat's-eye stones with a sharp, centered line, which are among the most distinctive gems in the world.

Spodumene.description: Spodumene family gemstones: kunzite, hiddenite and triphane. A lithium aluminum silicate with pink, green and yellow varieties. See the full list.
Spodumene.intro: Spodumene is a lithium aluminum silicate that forms flat, striated prismatic crystals in the monoclinic system, with a hardness of 6.5 to 7 and perfect cleavage. Kunzite is the pink to lilac variety, colored by manganese, and hiddenite is the rare emerald-green one, colored by chromium. Yellow and clear spodumene are also cut as gems. Kunzite is known for fading with long exposure to strong light, so collectors keep it in shade. Major sources include Afghanistan, Brazil and Madagascar, and spodumene is also an important lithium ore. Explore the group below. Its soft pastel colors and clear crystals have made it a favorite among collectors since it was named in the early twentieth century.

Zeolite.description: Zeolite family crystals: stilbite, apophyllite, natrolite and heulandite. Delicate hydrated silicates that form in volcanic cavities and geodes.
Zeolite.intro: Zeolites are hydrated aluminum silicates that grow in cavities of volcanic rock, often alongside agate, calcite and quartz. They are generally soft to moderately hard, from 3.5 to 5.5, and many are light and fragile. Apophyllite forms glassy square crystals, stilbite makes sheaf-like sprays, and natrolite creates fine, needle-like groups. India's Deccan Traps are a world-famous source, along with Iceland, Brazil and Oregon. Collectors like zeolites for their bright, delicate habits. Explore the group below. Handle specimens by the matrix rather than the crystals, and keep them away from heat, which can dry out or crack them.

Calcite & Carbonates.description: Calcite and carbonate crystals: calcite, aragonite, rhodochrosite, malachite and more. Soft, colorful minerals loved for their shapes and glowing tones.
Calcite & Carbonates.intro: Carbonates are minerals built around the carbonate group, and calcite is the best known, with a hardness of 3 and perfect rhombohedral cleavage. Aragonite, rhodochrosite, smithsonite, malachite, azurite and dolomite are relatives. They fizz in acid, which is one way geologists identify them. Calcite forms in an astonishing range of colors and shapes, from honey-yellow rhombs to pink and orange masses. Because most are soft and some are toxic, collectors treat them carefully. Explore the group below. Handle them gently, keep them away from acids such as vinegar and lemon juice, and store each piece with some padding.

Fluorite.description: Fluorite crystals: cubic calcium fluoride in purple, green, blue and rainbow banding. Prized by collectors and loved for its glassy color. See the full list.
Fluorite.intro: Fluorite is calcium fluoride, forming glassy cubes and octahedra in the cubic system, with a hardness of 4 and perfect cleavage. It comes in nearly every color, often with several in one specimen, and rainbow fluorite with purple, green and clear bands is a favorite. Some fluorite glows under ultraviolet light, which is where the word fluorescence comes from. Classic localities include England, China, Mexico and Illinois. Because it is soft and cleaves easily, fluorite is better as a display piece than in rings. Explore the group below. Keep it out of strong sun, which can fade the color, and wrap it in cloth to protect its soft surface.

Sulfates.description: Sulfate crystals: selenite, gypsum, celestite and barite. Soft minerals built on the sulfate group, loved for their glassy blades and pale colors.
Sulfates.intro: Sulfates are minerals built around the sulfate group. Gypsum is the best known, appearing as clear selenite blades, pearly satin spar and desert rose. Celestite forms pale blue crystals, and barite can make tabular, heavy crystals. Most sulfates are soft, with a hardness of 1.5 to 3.5, and gypsum even scratches with a fingernail, so they should be kept dry and handled gently. Large selenite crystals in Mexico's Naica cave are among the biggest ever found. Collectors treasure the pale, luminous look of the group. Explore the group below. Keep them away from water and humidity, which can cloud or dissolve the softer members of the group.

Phosphates.description: Phosphate crystals: apatite, turquoise, vivianite and variscite. A varied group of minerals built on the phosphate group, from blues to greens.
Phosphates.intro: Phosphate minerals include apatite, turquoise, variscite, vivianite, pyromorphite and wavellite. Apatite has a hardness of 5 and occurs in blue, green and yellow, while turquoise is a hydrated copper aluminum phosphate valued for its sky-blue color. Many phosphates grow in the weathered zones of ore deposits and as fine radiating crusts. Most are soft or brittle, and a few contain heavy metals, so care is needed. Teeth and bones are also made of an apatite relative. Collectors enjoy the vivid colors of the group. Explore the group below. Keep them away from heat, water and harsh cleaners, and store each piece separately to prevent scratches.

Copper Minerals.description: Copper mineral crystals: malachite, azurite, chrysocolla and dioptase. Vivid blue and green stones that need careful handling and no water. See the full list.
Copper Minerals.intro: Copper minerals form where copper ore weathers, giving some of the most vivid greens and blues in the mineral world. Malachite, azurite, chrysocolla, dioptase, turquoise and native copper belong here. Most are soft to moderate, with hardness around 2 to 4.5, and many are toxic if the dust is swallowed, so wash hands and never make elixirs. Collectors prize the banded patterns of malachite and the deep blue of azurite. Notable sources include Congo, Arizona, Morocco and Namibia. Explore the group below. Display them dry, out of reach of children and pets, and wash your hands after every handling.

Mica.description: Mica family crystals: lepidolite, muscovite, biotite and fuchsite. Sheet silicates that peel into thin, flexible, shimmering layers. See the full list.
Mica.intro: Micas are sheet silicates that split into thin, flexible, elastic flakes, giving them a distinctive shine. Muscovite is the pale, clear form, biotite is dark, lepidolite is lilac and contains lithium, and fuchsite is green from chromium. Hardness is low, between 2 and 3, so they scratch and flake easily. Mica has been used for centuries as a window material, in cosmetics and in electrical parts. Collectors like the glittery books and plates found in pegmatites. Explore the group below. Display them in a protected spot, because even a light touch can lift thin layers from the surface.

Serpentine.description: Serpentine family stones: green and gold serpentines, antigorite and more. Soft magnesium silicates with waxy, snake-skin-like patterns. See the full list.
Serpentine.intro: Serpentine is a group of magnesium silicate minerals named for their mottled, snake-skin-like patterns. Antigorite, lizardite and chrysotile are the main types, with hardness of 2.5 to 5.5. Serpentine is usually green, but can be yellow, brown or nearly black, with a smooth, waxy feel that carves well. Varieties include bowenite, a hard, translucent green, and the stone sold as New Jade. One fibrous form, chrysotile, is an asbestos mineral, so quality control matters when buying raw material. Explore the group below. Choose polished pieces from reliable sellers, and store them where they will not be knocked by harder stones.

Silicates (Other).description: Other silicate crystals: kyanite, iolite, peridot, zircon and many more. A diverse set of silicates that do not fit the larger gem families.
Silicates (Other).intro: Silicates are the largest class of minerals, and this group gathers the ones that do not belong to a bigger family. Peridot, kyanite, iolite, sphene, zircon, charoite, sugilite, epidote and many more are found here. Hardness ranges from 4 to 8, and each has its own structure and use. Kyanite forms blue blades with two different hardnesses, iolite changes color when viewed from different angles, and peridot is among the few gems that come in one color only. Collectors enjoy the variety. Explore the group below. Because the group is so diverse, check the individual stone for hardness, light sensitivity and care needs before buying.

Oxides.description: Oxide crystals: hematite, magnetite, rutile, cuprite and more. Dense minerals made of metals bonded with oxygen. Traditions and uses. See the full list.
Oxides.intro: Oxides are minerals in which a metal is combined with oxygen. Hematite and magnetite are iron oxides, rutile is titanium oxide, cuprite is copper oxide, and corundum and spinel are oxides too, though they usually have their own families. Oxides tend to be heavy and hard, with strong luster. Hematite has a reddish streak, magnetite is naturally magnetic, and rutile forms golden needles inside quartz. Many are important ores. Collectors love their weight, shine and clear crystal forms. Explore the group below. Many of them are durable, so they suit jewelry and hand-held stones, though a few are brittle or have sharp edges.

Sulfides.description: Sulfide crystals: pyrite, galena, sphalerite and chalcopyrite. Metallic minerals that form brilliant, often geometric crystals. See the full list.
Sulfides.intro: Sulfides combine metals with sulfur, and many have a bright metallic luster that surprises first-time collectors. Pyrite, known as fool's gold, forms perfect cubes and pyritohedrons, while galena shows heavy silver cubes and chalcopyrite has a brassy, iridescent tarnish. Hardness runs from 2.5 to 6.5. Many are ores of important metals, and several contain lead, arsenic or other heavy elements, so careful handling matters and elixirs should never be made. Collectors prize sharp, shining crystals from Peru, Spain and Missouri. Explore the group below. Keep them dry, since moisture and air can tarnish or break down some of them, and store each piece in its own box.

Native Elements.description: Native element crystals: gold, silver, copper, sulfur, bismuth and diamond. Minerals found in pure elemental form in nature. See the full list.
Native Elements.intro: Native elements are minerals made of a single element, found uncombined in nature. Gold, silver, copper, platinum, sulfur, graphite, diamond and bismuth are the best known. They vary hugely: diamond is the hardest natural substance at 10, while graphite is among the softest. Native copper can form branching, tree-like crystals, and bismuth grows rainbow-colored stair-step shapes. Collectors prize well-formed crystals and rare finds from Michigan, Siberia and South Africa. Explore the group below. Many are rare, and some are valuable for the metal alone, so a trusted dealer matters when buying the better pieces.

Iron Minerals.description: Iron mineral crystals: hematite, magnetite, goethite and limonite. Heavy, dark stones with a long history in tools, ornaments and charms. See the full list.
Iron Minerals.intro: Iron minerals are the ores that supply most of the world's iron and include hematite, magnetite, goethite and limonite. They are heavy for their size and often have a metallic or earthy luster, with hardness of 5 to 6.5. Hematite polishes to a mirror-like silver-grey, and magnetite is naturally attracted to magnets. Banded iron formations are some of the oldest rocks on Earth. Iron stones have been carved into beads and amulets since ancient times. Collectors enjoy the weight and shine. Explore the group below. Keep them dry, since moisture can cause surface rust, and expect a very noticeable weight when you hold one.

Volcanic Glass & Tektites.description: Volcanic glass and tektite stones: obsidian, moldavite and Libyan desert glass. Natural glass formed by fire and impact, without a crystal structure.
Volcanic Glass & Tektites.intro: Obsidian forms when felsic lava cools too fast for crystals to grow, leaving a natural volcanic glass with sharp, curved fractures. Tektites are glass formed when a meteorite impact melted surface rock, which then cooled as it flew through the air. Moldavite from Czechia, Libyan desert glass and Darwin glass are famous examples. These materials have no crystal structure, with hardness around 5 to 6. People have used obsidian for blades and mirrors since the Stone Age. Collectors prize rare tektite shapes. Explore the group below. Handle sharp edges with care, and be wary of imitations, which are common for the rarer tektite types.

Organic Gems.description: Organic gems: amber, pearl, coral, jet and ammolite. Materials formed by living things, from ancient resin to shells and fossil wood. See the full list.
Organic Gems.intro: Organic gems are made by living organisms rather than by geologic processes alone. Amber is fossil tree resin millions of years old, pearl and coral are made by marine animals, jet is a dense form of fossilized wood, and ammolite is the iridescent shell of an ancient ammonite. They are generally softer than mineral gems, with hardness of 2 to 4.5, and can be harmed by heat, chemicals and sweat. Collectors prize amber with insect inclusions and fine natural pearls. Explore the group below. Keep them away from heat, perfume and strong light, and wipe them gently with a soft dry cloth after wearing.

Rocks & Formations.description: Rock and formation stones: geodes, septarian, petrified wood and shungite. Natural mixtures and shapes rather than single-mineral crystals. See the full list.
Rocks & Formations.intro: Not every crystal collection item is a single mineral. Rocks are mixtures of minerals, and formations are shapes made by natural processes. Geodes, septarian nodules, petrified wood, lava stone, unakite, lapis lazuli, shungite and many more fall into this group. Hardness varies widely, since each piece is made of several things. Their appeal lies in pattern and story: a cut geode shows hidden crystals, while petrified wood preserves the grain of a tree that lived long ago. Explore the group below. Because every piece is different, collectors usually buy by eye and keep a favorite in hand or on a shelf.

Man-made.description: Man-made crystals: opalite, goldstone, aura quartz and lab-grown stones. Created or enhanced in a lab or workshop, sold openly as such. See the full list.
Man-made.intro: Man-made crystals are created or enhanced by people rather than found whole in nature. Opalite is glass, goldstone is glass with copper crystals, aura quartz is natural quartz coated with metals, and synthetic gems are grown in a laboratory. Some, like lab-grown ruby, have the same chemistry as natural stones, while others are only imitations. They are usually affordable, bright and consistent in color. Honest sellers say clearly what is natural and what is not. Many people enjoy them for their color and use them in tradition just as they would a natural stone. Explore the group below. Because the materials are modern, there is no need for rarity, so enjoy them for color and affordability.

Earth.description: Earth element crystals in the healing tradition: dense, grounding stones linked to stability, patience, practicality and the body. See the full list.
Earth.intro: Earth is the element of stability, patience and practical living. In the crystal tradition, Earth stones are dense, dark or green, with a natural, solid feel: smoky quartz, black tourmaline, jasper, moss agate, malachite, hematite and petrified wood are typical. Astrologers link Earth to the signs Taurus, Virgo and Capricorn. Practitioners say Earth stones suit people who want to feel steady, finish tasks and slow down. They are often placed in the home, in gardens, on the floor or at the base of the spine in meditation. Many collectors like their rich, warm colors. Explore the Earth crystals below.

Water.description: Water element crystals in the healing tradition: smooth, flowing stones linked to emotion, intuition, empathy and calm. Traditions and uses.
Water.intro: Water is the element of emotion, intuition and flow. In the crystal tradition, Water stones are blue, sea-green or pearly white, with a smooth or glowing look: aquamarine, moonstone, blue lace agate, larimar, pearl, selenite and calcite are typical. Astrologers link Water to Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces. Practitioners say Water stones suit emotional reflection, empathy, dream work and quiet evenings. They are often placed near bedrooms, bathrooms or by the sea. Always check whether a stone can safely touch water first, since many cannot. Explore the Water crystals below. Many stones in this group are soft, so check care instructions before putting any near water.

Fire.description: Fire element crystals in the healing tradition: warm red, orange and gold stones linked to drive, passion, courage and creative spark. See the full list.
Fire.intro: Fire is the element of energy, passion and action. In the crystal tradition, Fire stones are red, orange or golden: carnelian, ruby, garnet, red jasper, sunstone, citrine and tiger's eye are typical. Astrologers link Fire to Aries, Leo and Sagittarius. Practitioners say Fire stones suit motivation, courage, creative projects and mornings that need a push. They are often worn as jewelry or placed on a desk, near a hearth or in a sunny window, though some fade in strong light. Many collectors enjoy their warm, glowing colors. Explore the Fire crystals below.

Air.description: Air element crystals in the healing tradition: light, clear and pale stones linked to thought, communication, curiosity and fresh perspective.
Air.intro: Air is the element of thought, communication and movement. In the crystal tradition, Air stones are clear, pale blue, yellow or white, and often light or airy in feel: clear quartz, fluorite, celestite, sodalite, citrine, amazonite and apophyllite are typical. Astrologers link Air to Gemini, Libra and Aquarius. Practitioners say Air stones suit study, writing, conversations and any situation that needs fresh ideas. They are often placed near windows, on desks or carried while traveling. Collectors enjoy their pale, bright look. Explore the Air crystals below. Many of these stones are light-colored, so keep them away from dust and strong sun.

Spirit.description: Spirit element crystals in the healing tradition: high, clear and radiant stones linked to meditation, spiritual connection and inner stillness.
Spirit.intro: Spirit, sometimes called Akasha or Aether, is the fifth element in many traditions, joining Earth, Water, Fire and Air. In the crystal tradition, Spirit stones are clear, white, violet or iridescent, often rare or unusual: selenite, moldavite, danburite, Herkimer diamond, phenacite, lepidolite and storm-related stones belong here. Practitioners say they suit meditation, prayer, ritual and quiet reflection. They are often placed on an altar or held at the crown of the head. Some collectors treat them as the center of an elemental set, with one stone for each of the other four around them. Explore the Spirit crystals below.
